Name: negation_late_override
Title: Retrieve First, Negate Later: Why LLMs Struggle to Suppress Facts They Just Retrieved
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM answers a negated or counterfactual query ('Which of these is NOT a country in Europe?', 'Paris is not the capital of __'), it first retrieves the affirmative fact using the same mid-layer machinery as the positive query, and only attempts to invert/suppress it via a late, shallow, and error-prone operation. We hypothesize that (1) affirmative retrieval is negation-blind (the correct answer to the un-negated query is decodable in mid layers regardless of the negation cue), (2) negation errors arise specifically when this late override fails to suppress the retrieved affirmative direction, and (3) a lightweight 'negation-completion' intervention that amplifies the suppression of the retrieved affirmative direction restores correct behavior without weight edits.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs handle negation poorly (Kassner & Schutze 2020 'Negated and Misprimed Probes'; Ettinger 2020), and factual-recall circuit work (Geva et al. 2023; Fierro et al. 2024) dissects positive subject-attribute recall as MLP-enrichment + attention-extraction. Cross-lingual work (Wang et al. 2025) shows late-layer transitions cause failures. RAG-shortcut work (Wadhwa et al. 2024) studies context-vs-parametric competition. None of these mechanistically characterize how a negation cue interacts with parametric retrieval: whether the model retrieves the affirmative fact regardless of negation and then must invert it. Our contribution is the first mechanistic account of negation as a *late override on top of negation-blind retrieval*, an example-level diagnostic distinguishing 'retrieved-but-failed-to-negate' from other errors, and a targeted negation-completion intervention. This is distinct from all prior negation-probing (behavioral) and factual-recall (positive-only) literature and from our other retrieval-mechanism proposals.
Abstract: Language models are notoriously unreliable on negated and counterfactual queries, yet why they fail remains mechanistically unclear. We propose that negation failures are not retrieval failures but *override* failures: given a negated query, the model first retrieves the relevant affirmative fact using the same mid-layer lookup machinery it uses for positive queries, and only afterward attempts to suppress or invert that retrieved answer via a late, shallow operation that frequently misfires. We test three claims on matched query pairs where only polarity differs ('X is the capital of __' vs. 'X is not the capital of __', and multiple-choice 'which is/is NOT'). First, using logit lens, linear probes, and activation patching, we test negation-blindness: whether the affirmative answer is decodable in mid layers regardless of the negation cue, and whether the negation cue is only integrated in late layers. Second, we partition negation errors into cases where the retrieved affirmative direction persists into the answer position (override failure) versus genuine knowledge gaps, and localize the layers/heads responsible for suppression via attention-knockout. Third, we introduce a training-free 'negation-completion' intervention: at the answer position we subtract (scaled) the retrieved affirmative-answer direction, testing whether negated-query accuracy improves without harming affirmative queries and without hallucination. Experiments span Pythia, Qwen2.5, and Llama-3 across scales, and we test whether the retrieve-then-override structure and its failure rate change with scale. This yields a mechanistic theory of negation failure and a cheap corrective probe.
Experiments: 1) BENCHMARK: Build ~4k matched query pairs differing only in polarity, over CounterFact/T-REx relations plus category-membership facts. Forms: (a) declarative affirmative vs. negated cloze ('Paris is the capital of __' vs. 'Paris is NOT the capital of __' -> expects a non-answer / different city), (b) multiple-choice 'which of these IS' vs. 'which is NOT' with 4 options and verifiable membership, (c) counterfactual assertions ('Even though Paris is not in France, it is in __'). Verify affirmative-query accuracy so we isolate items whose affirmative fact is stored. 2) NEGATION-BLINDNESS TEST: For negated queries, use logit lens and per-layer linear probes to test whether the AFFIRMATIVE answer token is decodable at mid layers (subject/answer position) despite the negation cue. Report the layer at which the negation cue first shifts the decoded answer (integration depth). Prediction: affirmative answer dominates mid layers; negation integrated only late. 3) ERROR PARTITION: On negated multiple-choice/cloze errors, classify each as (a) OVERRIDE FAILURE (model outputs the affirmative/true-positive item, i.e., the thing that IS the case, when asked what is NOT) vs. (b) genuine knowledge gap (affirmative not stored). Report fractions and how they vary across forms and scale. 4) MECHANISM LOCALIZATION: Use activation patching (affirmative vs. negated prompt) and attention-knockout to identify late-layer heads/positions that carry the negation cue and perform suppression; compare successful vs. failed negations to find where suppression breaks. 5) DIAGNOSTIC CLASSIFIER: Train a classifier on internal features to predict, before the answer, whether a negated query will suffer an override failure; report AUROC on held-out relations, incremental over a difficulty baseline. 6) NEGATION-COMPLETION INTERVENTION: At the answer position for negated queries, subtract (scaled by alpha) the retrieved affirmative-answer direction (difference-of-means direction that decodes the affirmative answer). Measure: negated-query accuracy gain, false-intervention rate on affirmative queries (must not degrade), hallucination rate on genuine-gap items (must not fabricate confident wrong negations), side effects on unrelated queries. Baselines: no intervention, CoT, explicit 'the answer must NOT be X' prompting, random-direction subtraction. 7) SCALING/GENERALIZATION: Repeat on Pythia (410M/1.4B/6.9B), Qwen2.5 (0.5B/7B), Llama-3 (8B); test whether negation integration depth, override-failure rate, and intervention gains change with scale, and whether the suppression direction transfers across relations. METRICS: mid-layer affirmative decodability (AUROC), negation-integration layer depth, override-failure fraction, localization effect sizes, diagnostic AUROC/incremental AUROC, intervention accuracy gain, false-intervention/hallucination rates, scaling trends.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Mid-layer decodability may overstate 'retrieval'; we require causal patching corroboration and treat decodability as necessary-not-sufficient. 2) Negated queries often have many valid answers (anything that is NOT the capital), making 'correct' fuzzy; we mitigate with multiple-choice forms (single correct 'NOT' option) and category-membership sets with verifiable ground truth. 3) Some negation failures may reflect prompt-format/instruction-following issues rather than retrieve-then-override; we compare across forms and include an instruction-tuned model to separate these. 4) The negation-completion intervention risks over-suppressing and harming affirmative queries; false-intervention and hallucination rates are explicit success criteria. 5) Effects may be architecture/scale specific (GQA vs MHA); we characterize across families rather than assume universality. 6) The affirmative-answer direction may be entangled with the negated answer for multi-answer relations; we restrict primary causal claims to near-functional relations and single-correct multiple-choice items.
